chapters.title: Chapter 3: Gold as a Macro Hedge

lessons.title: Why Gold Trades Differently From Every Other Commodity

children.text: Gold Isn't Really a Commodity. It's a Monetary Asset That Happens to Be Mined

Everything in Chapters 1 and 2 rested on a simple idea: a commodity's price is anchored by the cost of producing it, and supply that lags demand is what creates a boom or a bust. Gold breaks this framework almost entirely. Copper gets used up: turned into wire, pipe, motors, and eventually scrapped or landfilled. Gold, once mined, almost never leaves the world's stock. It gets melted down and reshaped, from jewellery to bars to coins and back again, but it does not get consumed the way oil is burned or copper is wired into a building. That single difference changes everything about how gold's price actually gets set.

body.text: Copper needs a factory to want it today. Gold just needs someone, anywhere in the world, to want to hold a little more of it than they did yesterday.

children.text: New mine supply adds a tiny fraction to the total pool of gold that already exists above ground. This is why a mine strike, a new discovery, or even a meaningful change in annual mine output barely moves the gold price, in sharp contrast to how a supply disruption moves oil or copper.

markDefs.definition: The ratio of existing stockpiles to annual new production. A high stock-to-flow ratio means new supply is a small share of what already exists, which makes the price far less sensitive to short-term production changes.

children.text: , and it is the single biggest reason gold's price is set by how badly people want to hold the existing pile, not by how much new gold miners can dig up this quarter.

body.title: Gold vs Oil and Industrial Metals

columns.label: Oil and Industrial Metals
points: Price anchored by cost of new production
Cycle driven by capex and the supply lag from Chapter 1
Tends to rise when global growth is strong (procyclical)

columns.label: Gold
points: Almost never consumed; the existing stock just changes hands
Price driven by the willingness to hold existing supply, not the cost of mining more
Cycle driven by real interest rates, currency moves, and macro sentiment
Often rises when growth is weak or uncertain (a hedge, not a growth bet)

children.text: The Single Biggest Lever: Real Interest Rates

Gold pays no interest and no dividend. Holding it means giving up whatever yield you could otherwise have earned on a bond. That opportunity cost is best measured by the real interest rate, the interest rate after subtracting expected inflation, and it is the closest thing gold has to a fundamental valuation anchor.

body.caption: When real rates fall, the cost of holding a zero-yield asset like gold falls with them, which tends to support the gold price. When real rates rise, gold has to compete against an increasingly attractive risk-free return, which tends to pressure it.

children.text: This is why gold traders watch US Treasury yields and inflation expectations as closely as they watch anything gold-specific. A surprise shift in expectations for future US interest rate cuts can move gold more than a genuine mine supply disruption ever would.
Two More Drivers: Central Banks and Indian Cultural Demand

body.caption: Two Demand Sources That Have Nothing to Do With Industrial Use

cells: Many central banks, including the RBI, have been consistent net buyers of gold in recent years, part of a broader move to diversify reserves away from heavy dollar concentration, a trend that accelerated after Russia's dollar and euro reserves were frozen following its 2022 invasion of Ukraine

India and China together account for a large share of global gold jewellery demand, with Indian buying tied closely to the wedding season and festivals such as Akshaya Tritiya and Dhanteras, creating a demand pattern with almost no equivalent in oil or metals

body.label: India's Gold Import Duty Cut
body.context: In the July 2024 Union Budget, the basic customs duty on gold and silver was cut sharply, a policy change that directly narrowed the gap between domestic and international gold prices and briefly boosted demand. Import duty rates are revised periodically, so check the current rate before assuming this figure still holds.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Driver Belongs to Gold?
body.question: Which of the following is most likely to move the gold price sharply while having little direct effect on the crude oil price?
options: A major new oil field discovery
A surprise shift in expectations for US interest rate cuts
A rise in Chinese steel demand
An OPEC+ decision to raise output
body.explanation: Gold has no industrial supply-demand mechanism like oil or steel. Its price responds most sharply to changes in real interest rate expectations, since that directly changes the opportunity cost of holding a zero-yield asset. The other three options are supply or demand shifts specific to oil or industrial metals, and would have little direct bearing on gold.

body.title: Show me: what stock-to-flow does and doesn't explain

children.text: A high stock-to-flow ratio explains why gold is resistant to short-term supply shocks: a mine closure or a bumper year of production is tiny relative to the existing 210,000-tonne pool, so it barely nudges price the way a similar percentage disruption would for oil or copper.

What it does not explain is the direction gold actually moves day to day, or why gold sometimes rallies for years and sometimes sits flat for a decade. That direction comes from the demand side: real interest rates, central bank buying, currency moves and crisis-driven safe-haven demand, all covered in this lesson, and expanded on in the next.

points: Gold is barely consumed, so its price is set by the willingness to hold the existing above-ground stock, not by the cost of mining more, which is why it does not follow the boom-bust framework from Chapters 1 and 2.
Real interest rates are gold's single biggest fundamental driver, because gold pays no yield and its opportunity cost rises and falls directly with the rate available on safe bonds.
Central bank reserve diversification and Indian and Chinese cultural demand add two more demand sources with no equivalent in oil or industrial metals.

The next lesson goes deeper on real rates and the dollar, the two variables that explain most of gold's medium-term moves, before Lesson 3 covers how to actually build gold exposure in an Indian portfolio.
